lessons.title: INSERT Basics
lessons.concept: INSERT adds new rows to a table. You can specify column names and corresponding values, or provide values for all columns in table order (when appropriate). Providing column names is clearer and safer when table structure changes.
lessons.formula: INSERT INTO table_name (col1, col2) VALUES (val1, val2); or INSERT INTO table_name VALUES (val1, val2, ...);
lessons.worked_example: INSERT INTO students (id, name) VALUES (1, 'Asha'); adds a new student row with id 1 and name Asha.
mistakes: Mismatch between number/order of columns and values
Inserting values that violate constraints (NOT NULL, UNIQUE, FK)
Forgetting quotes around string/date literals in SQL dialects that require them
lessons.provenance: Authored original lesson; not scraped. Requires independent verification before TRUSTED promotion.

lessons.title: UPDATE Basics
lessons.concept: UPDATE modifies existing rows in a table. The SET clause specifies new values for columns, and the WHERE clause determines which rows are affected. Without WHERE, all rows in the table are updated.
lessons.formula: UPDATE table_name SET col1 = val1, col2 = val2 WHERE condition;
lessons.worked_example: UPDATE students SET name = 'Anita' WHERE id = 1; changes the name only for the row with id 1.
mistakes: Omitting WHERE and unintentionally updating every row
Using = in WHERE incorrectly for NULL checks (use IS NULL/IS NOT NULL)
Setting wrong column values due to incorrect condition logic
lessons.provenance: Authored original lesson; not scraped. Requires independent verification before TRUSTED promotion.

lessons.title: DELETE and Safe Modification Practices
lessons.concept: DELETE removes rows from a table based on a condition. Like UPDATE, omitting WHERE deletes all rows (table structure remains). It is good practice to verify the target rows with a SELECT using the same WHERE condition before running UPDATE/DELETE.
lessons.formula: DELETE FROM table_name WHERE condition; (Be careful: DELETE FROM table_name; removes all rows.)
lessons.worked_example: SELECT * FROM students WHERE id = 1; then DELETE FROM students WHERE id = 1; confirms and removes only that row.
mistakes: Omitting WHERE and deleting all rows by accident
Confusing DELETE (removes rows) with DROP (removes table/object)
Not considering foreign key constraints that may block deletion

practice.question: Which SQL command is used to add new rows to a table?
practice.explanation: INSERT adds new records (rows) into a table.

practice.question: What is the risk of running UPDATE without a WHERE clause?

options.B: All rows in the table are updated
options.D: Only the first row is updated

practice.explanation: Without a WHERE condition, UPDATE applies the SET changes to every row in the table.

practice.question: Which statement correctly updates name to 'Ravi' for id 5 in table users?

options.A: UPDATE users SET name = 'Ravi' WHERE id = 5;
options.B: INSERT INTO users SET name = 'Ravi' WHERE id = 5;
options.C: UPDATE users WHERE id = 5 SET name = 'Ravi';
options.D: DELETE users SET name = 'Ravi' WHERE id = 5;

practice.explanation: Correct syntax is UPDATE table SET ... WHERE .... This modifies existing rows matching the condition.

practice.explanation: DELETE removes rows that satisfy the WHERE condition. Only rows with dept = 'HR' are removed.

practice.question: Which command removes rows but does not remove the table structure?
practice.explanation: DELETE removes data rows from a table. DROP TABLE removes the table definition and its data; ALTER/CREATE modify or create structures.

practice.question: Which SQL statement adds a new row to a table?
practice.explanation: INSERT INTO adds new rows. UPDATE modifies existing rows, DELETE removes rows, and ALTER changes the table structure.

practice.question: Which statement permanently removes all rows from a table but keeps its structure?
practice.explanation: DELETE without a WHERE clause removes every row while retaining columns/constraints; DROP removes the table itself. TRUNCATE also empties the table (usually faster, minimally logged).

questions.question: To safely modify specific rows, UPDATE and DELETE statements should usually include:

questions.question: If an INSERT violates a UNIQUE constraint, what typically happens?

options.B: The insert is rejected with a constraint error

questions.explanation: Constraints enforce data integrity; inserting a duplicate value into a UNIQUE-constrained column violates the rule and the operation fails.

questions.question: What is the effect of running 'UPDATE students SET marks = marks + 5' with no WHERE clause?

options.B: Every row in the table gets marks increased by 5

questions.explanation: Without WHERE, UPDATE applies to all rows - a classic accidental-mass-update hazard. Always filter with WHERE unless updating the whole table is intended.

questions.question: Which clause filters rows before an UPDATE or DELETE is applied?
questions.explanation: WHERE selects which rows the statement affects. GROUP BY aggregates, ORDER BY sorts results, and HAVING filters groups after aggregation.

questions.question: Why should 'DELETE FROM table' generally be preferred over 'DROP TABLE' when rows must be removed but data may be needed later?

options.B: DELETE keeps the table structure and can be rolled back if uncommitted

questions.explanation: DELETE removes data but preserves schema and constraints and (in a transaction) can be rolled back; DROP destroys the table definition, so recovery requires recreating structure and redefining constraints.
